name: Bangladesh Liberation War
summary: After Pakistan's military government refused to hand power to the Awami League, which had won the 1970 election, it launched a crackdown in East Pakistan in March 1971 and Bengali nationalists declared independence. A nine-month guerrilla war, a massive refugee flight to India and finally a two-week Indian invasion in December ended with the surrender of Pakistani forces in Dhaka and the birth of Bangladesh. Estimates of the dead range from several hundred thousand to about three million.

sides.name: Pakistan
leaders: Lt Gen. A. A. K. Niazi

steps.label: 25 to 27 Mar 1971
steps.title: Operation Searchlight
steps.text: On the night of 25 March the Pakistani army under Lt Gen. Tikka Khan struck in Dhaka against Awami League leaders, students and Bengali police and soldiers, and arrested Sheikh Mujibur Rahman. Independence was proclaimed on 26 March and broadcast from Chittagong, and mutinous Bengali units fell back toward the Indian border as the army fanned out to retake the towns.

events.name: Operation Searchlight
events.text: The army's crackdown in Dhaka began a campaign of mass killing and arrests across East Pakistan.

events.name: Declaration of independence
events.text: Independence was proclaimed on 26 March and announced over the radio from Chittagong.

steps.label: Apr to Nov 1971
steps.title: Guerrilla war and refugee crisis
steps.text: A government in exile was sworn in at Mujibnagar in April, and Col. M. A. G. Osmani organised the Mukti Bahini guerrillas from bases in India. Lt Gen. A. A. K. Niazi took command of Pakistani forces, while about ten million refugees crossed into India. In August India signed a friendship treaty with the Soviet Union and stepped up support for the insurgents.

moves.label: Mukti Bahini raids from the west

moves.commander: Lt Gen. A. A. K. Niazi
moves.label: Garrisons pushed to the border

events.name: Mujibnagar government sworn in
events.text: The Provisional Government of Bangladesh took its oath in a mango grove near the Indian border.

events.name: Indo-Soviet Treaty
events.text: India gained Soviet diplomatic backing against outside intervention.

steps.label: 3 to 15 Dec 1971
steps.title: India enters the war
steps.text: Pakistani air strikes on Indian airfields on 3 December brought open war. In the east, Indian corps and Mukti Bahini units under Lt Gen. Jagjit Singh Aurora drove in from three sides, bypassing strongpoints and crossing the Meghna toward Dhaka, while an airborne drop at Tangail cut off retreating troops. In the west the two armies fought along the border and in Kashmir.

moves.commander: Lt Gen. A. A. K. Niazi
moves.label: Pull back on Dhaka

events.name: Battle of Longewala
events.text: A small Indian post, backed by air strikes, held off a Pakistani armoured thrust into Rajasthan.

events.name: Tangail airdrop
events.text: Indian paratroopers landed behind Pakistani lines to block the road to Dhaka.

steps.label: 16 Dec 1971 to 1972
steps.title: Surrender in Dhaka
steps.text: On 16 December Lt Gen. Niazi signed the instrument of surrender before Lt Gen. Aurora in Dhaka, and about 93,000 Pakistani personnel became prisoners of war. A ceasefire in the west followed the next day, Sheikh Mujibur Rahman returned to lead Bangladesh in January 1972, and the Simla Agreement of July 1972 set terms for peace between India and Pakistan.

moves.label: Indian and Bangladeshi forces enter Dhaka

events.name: Pakistani surrender in Dhaka
events.text: The surrender at the Ramna Race Course ended the war and confirmed Bangladesh's independence.

events.name: Simla Agreement
events.text: India and Pakistan agreed to settle disputes bilaterally and returned captured land in the west.

name: Yom Kippur War
summary: On 6 October 1973, Yom Kippur, Egypt and Syria launched a surprise attack to recover the Sinai and the Golan Heights, held by Israel since 1967. After early Arab gains Israel stopped the Syrians, crossed the Suez Canal and surrounded the Egyptian Third Army before superpower pressure imposed a ceasefire. The war triggered the Arab oil embargo and opened the diplomacy that led to the 1979 Egypt-Israel peace treaty.

steps.label: 6 to 7 Oct 1973
steps.title: Operation Badr
steps.text: Egypt's Second and Third Armies crossed the Suez Canal under a heavy barrage, breached the Bar Lev Line and dug in on the east bank behind a screen of anti-tank and anti-aircraft missiles. At the same time about 1,400 Syrian tanks attacked the thinly held Golan Heights and in the south broke through almost to the Sea of Galilee.

fronts.label: Golan ceasefire line before the war

events.name: Crossing of the Suez Canal
events.text: Egyptian engineers bridged the canal and overran most Bar Lev strongpoints within hours.

events.name: Valley of Tears
events.text: A few dozen Israeli tanks held the northern Golan against repeated Syrian assaults.

steps.label: 8 to 14 Oct 1973
steps.title: Israel recovers
steps.text: Mobilised Israeli reserves threw the Syrians back across the ceasefire line by 10 October and pushed toward Damascus, where Iraqi and Jordanian forces joined the defence. An Israeli counterattack in Sinai on 8 October failed, but when Egypt advanced beyond its missile cover on 14 October its armoured attack was beaten off with heavy losses. Both sides were resupplied, Israel by a US airlift and the Arab states by the Soviet Union.

fronts.label: Golan front after the Israeli advance

events.name: Tank battle of 14 October
events.text: Egypt lost some 250 tanks attacking toward the Sinai passes.

events.name: Arab oil embargo
events.text: Arab oil producers cut output and embargoed the United States, quadrupling oil prices.

steps.label: 15 to 25 Oct 1973
steps.title: Across the canal
steps.text: Israeli divisions under Ariel Sharon and Avraham Adan forced a crossing at Deversoir after fierce fighting at the Chinese Farm and spread out on the west bank, destroying air defences. Adan's tanks drove south to the outskirts of Suez, cutting off the Egyptian Third Army. UN Security Council Resolution 338 called a ceasefire on 22 October, which took hold on 25 October after a brief US-Soviet crisis.

events.name: Battle of the Chinese Farm
events.text: Costly night fighting opened the corridor to Israel's canal bridgehead.

events.name: Encirclement of the Third Army
events.text: Some 30,000 Egyptian soldiers on the east bank were cut off when the ceasefire took hold.

events.name: UN Resolution 338
events.text: The Security Council demanded a ceasefire and negotiations under Resolution 242.

steps.label: 1974 to 1979
steps.title: From disengagement to peace
steps.text: US mediation under Henry Kissinger produced disengagement agreements with Egypt in January 1974 and with Syria in May 1974, pulling Israeli forces back from the canal and Quneitra. Egypt's partial success gave Sadat room for direct diplomacy, leading to the Camp David Accords in 1978 and the 1979 peace treaty under which Israel returned the Sinai.

events.name: Sinai disengagement agreement
events.text: Israel withdrew east of the canal and a UN buffer zone separated the armies.

events.name: Golan disengagement agreement
events.text: Israel returned Quneitra and a UN force took over a buffer zone on the Golan.

name: Lebanese Civil War
summary: Tensions over power-sharing between Lebanon's Christian and Muslim communities and over armed Palestinian groups in the country erupted into civil war in 1975. Shifting coalitions of militias fought for fifteen years while Syria and Israel intervened, Israel invading in 1982 and Syria keeping troops in much of the country. The 1989 Taif Agreement and Syria's defeat of Gen. Michel Aoun in 1990 ended the war, which killed an estimated 120,000 to 150,000 people.

sides.name: Christian militias (Lebanese Front) and, in 1982, Israel

steps.label: 1975 to 1976
steps.title: The war begins
steps.text: After gunmen fired on a church in Ain el-Remmaneh, Phalangist militiamen ambushed a bus carrying Palestinians on 13 April 1975, setting off fighting between Christian militias and the Lebanese National Movement allied with the PLO. Beirut split along the Green Line, and both sides committed massacres. In June 1976 Syria sent in its army, at first to stop the leftist and Palestinian advance, and Christian forces took the Tel al-Zaatar camp.

moves.label: LNM and PLO offensive in the mountains

events.name: Ain el-Remmaneh bus attack
events.text: The killing of bus passengers is taken as the start of the war.

events.name: Siege of Tel al-Zaatar
events.text: Christian militias besieged and overran the Palestinian camp, killing many civilians.

events.name: Syrian intervention
events.text: Syrian troops moved in and later stayed as the core of the Arab Deterrent Force.

steps.label: Jun to Sep 1982
steps.title: Israel invades
steps.text: After a 1978 incursion and years of PLO attacks from the south, Israel invaded on 6 June 1982, its columns driving up the coast to Beirut and fighting Syrian forces in the Bekaa. West Beirut was besieged until the PLO agreed to evacuate to Tunis in August. President-elect Bashir Gemayel was assassinated in September, and Lebanese Forces militiamen then killed hundreds of civilians in the Sabra and Shatila camps.

events.name: Siege of Beirut
events.text: Ten weeks of siege and bombardment ended with the PLO's departure from Lebanon.

events.name: Battle of Sultan Yacoub
events.text: Syrian forces stopped an Israeli armoured advance in the Bekaa.

events.name: Sabra and Shatila massacre
events.text: Militiamen killed hundreds and possibly thousands of Palestinian and Lebanese civilians.

steps.label: 1983 to 1984
steps.title: Multinational force and the Mountain War
steps.text: US, French and Italian troops arrived to support the new government of Amin Gemayel, but suicide bombings of the US Marine and French barracks in October 1983 killed 299 servicemen. In the Chouf mountains Walid Jumblatt's Druze militia defeated the Lebanese Forces, and in February 1984 Amal and Druze fighters took West Beirut. The multinational force withdrew and Israel pulled back toward the south.

moves.label: Lebanese army and Lebanese Forces fall back

events.name: Beirut barracks bombings
events.text: Truck bombs killed 241 US and 58 French servicemen, hastening the force's withdrawal.

events.name: Mountain War
events.text: Druze forces drove Christian militias out of most of the Chouf.

events.name: 6 February uprising
events.text: Amal and Druze militias took control of West Beirut from the army.

steps.label: 1985 to 1988
steps.title: Wars within the war
steps.text: Israel withdrew in 1985 to a security zone in the south held with the South Lebanon Army, while the Shia militia Hezbollah, backed by Iran, fought it there. Syrian-backed Amal besieged Palestinian camps in the War of the Camps and later fought Hezbollah, and Syrian troops returned to West Beirut in 1987. Kidnappings of foreigners and car bombings were frequent.

moves.label: Syrian troops return to West Beirut

events.name: War of the Camps
events.text: Amal sieges of Sabra, Shatila and Burj el-Barajneh lasted on and off until 1988.

events.name: Israel withdraws to the security zone
events.text: Israel kept a strip of the south with its allied South Lebanon Army until 2000.

steps.label: 1989 to 1990
steps.title: Taif and the end of the war
steps.text: With two rival governments, Gen. Michel Aoun declared a war of liberation against Syria in 1989, shelling and being shelled for months. The Taif Agreement of October 1989 rebalanced power between the communities, but Aoun rejected it and fought the Lebanese Forces of Samir Geagea in 1990. On 13 October 1990 Syrian forces stormed the presidential palace at Baabda, Aoun took refuge in the French embassy, and the militias other than Hezbollah were disarmed.

events.name: Taif Agreement
events.text: Lebanese MPs meeting in Saudi Arabia agreed a new power-sharing formula.

events.name: Fall of Baabda
events.text: Syrian and allied Lebanese army forces ousted Aoun, ending the fighting.

name: Soviet-Afghan War
summary: In December 1979 the Soviet Union invaded Afghanistan to prop up the communist government against a growing Islamist rebellion. For nearly a decade Soviet and Afghan government forces held the cities and roads while mujahideen groups, armed through Pakistan by the United States, Saudi Arabia and others, controlled much of the countryside. The Soviets withdrew in 1989 after about 15,000 deaths, while perhaps a million or more Afghans died and some five million became refugees.

steps.label: Mar to Dec 1979
steps.title: The Soviet invasion
steps.text: The communist government that seized power in 1978 faced spreading revolts, including a rising in Herat in March 1979. On 27 December Soviet special forces stormed the Tajbeg Palace, killed President Hafizullah Amin and installed Babrak Karmal, while the 40th Army crossed the Amu Darya at Termez and drove over the Salang Pass to Kabul, with a second column from Kushka to Herat and Kandahar.

events.name: Herat uprising
events.text: A revolt in Herat, put down at great cost, showed how weak the government's hold had become.

events.name: Operation Storm-333
events.text: Soviet commandos stormed the palace and killed Amin.

steps.label: 1980 to 1985
steps.title: Cities against countryside
steps.text: Over 100,000 Soviet troops held Kabul, the main towns and the ring road, while mujahideen groups based in Pakistan ambushed convoys and raided garrisons. Ahmad Shah Massoud beat off repeated Soviet offensives into the Panjshir Valley, which commanded the Salang highway. Bombing and sweeps emptied whole districts, and refugees poured into Pakistan and Iran.

events.name: Panjshir offensives
events.text: Nine Soviet offensives failed to destroy Massoud's forces in the valley.

steps.label: 1986 to Jan 1988
steps.title: Stingers and stalemate
steps.text: Mikhail Gorbachev called the war a bleeding wound, and in 1986 Mohammad Najibullah replaced Karmal and offered national reconciliation. US-supplied Stinger missiles, first used near Jalalabad in September 1986, made low flying costly for Soviet aircraft. Soviet operations could still win set battles, such as the relief of besieged Khost under Lt Gen. Boris Gromov in Operation Magistral, but not the war.

events.name: Battle of Zhawar
events.text: Afghan and Soviet forces overran a major mujahideen base near the border, then withdrew.

events.name: First Stinger shootdowns
events.text: Mujahideen shot down Soviet helicopters with shoulder-fired missiles near Jalalabad.

events.name: Operation Magistral
events.text: A large Soviet offensive reopened the road to Khost.

steps.label: Apr 1988 to Feb 1989
steps.title: The Soviet withdrawal
steps.text: The Geneva Accords of April 1988 committed the Soviet Union to leave. Half its troops left by August 1988 and the rest followed over the winter, back along the Salang highway and the western road. On 15 February 1989 Lt Gen. Boris Gromov walked last across the Friendship Bridge into Soviet Uzbekistan.

events.name: Geneva Accords
events.text: Afghanistan, Pakistan, the US and the USSR signed agreements setting the timetable for withdrawal.

events.name: Last Soviet troops leave
events.text: The withdrawal ended at the Friendship Bridge over the Amu Darya.

steps.label: Mar 1989 to 1992
steps.title: The government holds on
steps.text: Without Soviet troops but with Soviet supplies, Najibullah's government defeated a large mujahideen assault on Jalalabad in 1989. It survived until aid ended with the Soviet collapse, and in April 1992 mujahideen forces entered Kabul, after which the factions fought each other for the capital.

events.name: Battle of Jalalabad
events.text: Government forces held the city against months of mujahideen attacks.

name: Central American civil wars
summary: From 1979 Nicaragua, El Salvador and Guatemala were torn by civil wars rooted in inequality and military rule and sharpened by the Cold War. In Nicaragua the Sandinistas overthrew Somoza and then fought US-backed Contra rebels, while in El Salvador and Guatemala leftist guerrillas fought US-backed military governments whose campaigns killed large numbers of civilians. Regional peace plans ended the wars between 1990 and 1996, after some 300,000 deaths across the three countries.

steps.label: Jun to Jul 1979
steps.title: The Sandinista revolution
steps.text: A broad uprising led by the Sandinista National Liberation Front (FSLN) brought down the Somoza dynasty in Nicaragua. While Edén Pastora's southern front pinned the National Guard near the Costa Rican border, insurrections took city after city, and Anastasio Somoza fled on 17 July. Two days later the Sandinistas entered Managua.

events.name: Fall of Somoza
events.text: The FSLN took power in Managua, ending more than four decades of Somoza family rule.

steps.label: 1980 to 1983
steps.title: War in El Salvador and the Guatemalan highlands
steps.text: In El Salvador Archbishop Óscar Romero was shot dead in March 1980 and five guerrilla groups united as the FMLN, whose January 1981 offensive failed but left it holding rural zones in Chalatenango and Morazán. Army sweeps there included the El Mozote massacre. In Guatemala the army under Romeo Lucas García and then Efraín Ríos Montt waged a scorched-earth campaign against the URNG guerrillas and Maya villages in the highlands.

moves.label: Guatemalan army into the Ixil highlands

events.name: Assassination of Archbishop Romero
events.text: Romero was killed while saying Mass, a killing a UN truth commission tied to a death squad.

events.name: El Mozote massacre
events.text: Soldiers killed about 800 villagers in northern Morazán.

events.name: Highland massacres
events.text: Hundreds of Maya villages were destroyed in the army's counterinsurgency campaign.

steps.label: 1982 to 1987
steps.title: The Contra war
steps.text: The United States funded and trained the Contras, built around former National Guard officers, who raided northern Nicaragua from bases in Honduras under Enrique Bermúdez while a southern group operated from Costa Rica. The Sandinista army grew rapidly with conscription and Cuban and Soviet arms. The CIA mined Nicaraguan harbours in 1984, Congress cut off military aid, and the secret diversion of arms-sale money revealed in 1986 became the Iran-Contra affair.

events.name: Mining of Nicaraguan harbours
events.text: The International Court of Justice later ruled the US support for the Contras unlawful.

events.name: Iran-Contra affair
events.text: Revelations of covert arms sales funding the Contras led to a political scandal in the US.

steps.label: 1987 to 1992
steps.title: Esquipulas and peace in Nicaragua and El Salvador
steps.text: Costa Rican president Óscar Arias brokered the Esquipulas II accord of 1987, committing the region's presidents to ceasefires and elections. In Nicaragua the Sandinistas lost the February 1990 election to Violeta Chamorro and the Contras demobilised. In El Salvador the FMLN's November 1989 offensive reached San Salvador, soldiers murdered six Jesuit priests, and the stalemate led to the Chapultepec peace accords of 1992.

events.name: Esquipulas II
events.text: Central American presidents agreed a framework for ending the wars.

events.name: 1989 FMLN offensive
events.text: The guerrillas fought in the capital for weeks, showing neither side could win.

events.name: Chapultepec Peace Accords
events.text: The FMLN disarmed and became a political party, and the army was reduced and reformed.

steps.label: 1990 to 1996
steps.title: Guatemala's long war ends
steps.text: Guatemala's war, which began in 1960, continued at lower intensity while the government and the URNG negotiated under UN mediation. The Agreement on a Firm and Lasting Peace was signed in Guatemala City on 29 December 1996. A UN-backed truth commission later estimated 200,000 dead or disappeared in Guatemala and attributed most violations to state forces.

moves.label: URNG in the north and highlands

events.name: Nicaraguan election
events.text: Violeta Chamorro's victory brought a peaceful transfer of power from the Sandinistas.

events.name: Guatemalan Peace Accords
events.text: The final agreement ended 36 years of civil war.

name: Iran-Iraq War
summary: Iraq under Saddam Hussein invaded revolutionary Iran in September 1980, seeking the Shatt al-Arab waterway and Khuzestan and fearing the spread of Iran's revolution. Iran drove the invaders out by 1982 and then pushed into Iraq in costly offensives, while both sides attacked cities and oil tankers and Iraq used chemical weapons. The war ended in a UN ceasefire in 1988 with the borders unchanged and hundreds of thousands dead.

steps.label: Sep to Dec 1980
steps.title: Iraq invades
steps.text: On 22 September 1980 Iraqi aircraft struck Iranian airfields and divisions crossed the border on a broad front, the main effort into oil-rich Khuzestan. Khorramshahr fell after a month of street fighting and Abadan was besieged, but the advance stalled short of Ahvaz and Dezful as Revolutionary Guards and the regular army stiffened.

events.name: Battle of Khorramshahr
events.text: Iraqi troops took the port city after weeks of house-to-house fighting.

events.name: Siege of Abadan
events.text: Abadan and its refinery held out until Iran broke the siege in September 1981.

steps.label: Sep 1981 to Jun 1982
steps.title: Iran strikes back
steps.text: Iranian counteroffensives combining the army with masses of Revolutionary Guard and Basij volunteers broke the siege of Abadan, retook Bostan and in March 1982 routed Iraqi forces near Dezful. In May Iran recaptured Khorramshahr, taking about 19,000 prisoners. Saddam pulled his remaining troops back to the border, but Iran's leaders chose to carry the war into Iraq.

events.name: Operation Fath ol-Mobin
events.text: Iran destroyed several Iraqi divisions west of Dezful and Shush.

events.name: Liberation of Khorramshahr
events.text: Iran retook the city on 24 May, the turning point of the war.

steps.label: Jul 1982 to 1986
steps.title: Human waves and the war of attrition
steps.text: Iran's offensives toward Basra in 1982 and through the Hawizeh marshes in 1984 cost tens of thousands of lives for little ground, as Iraq dug in behind flooded barriers and used mustard and nerve gas. Both sides fired missiles at each other's cities, and from 1984 attacked tankers in the Gulf. In February 1986 Iranian troops crossed the Shatt al-Arab and seized the Faw peninsula.

events.name: Operation Ramadan
events.text: Iran's first major offensive into Iraq failed before Basra's defences.

events.name: Battle of the Marshes
events.text: Iran seized the Majnoon oil islands while Iraq used chemical weapons on a large scale.

events.name: First Battle of al-Faw
events.text: Iran's capture of Faw cut Iraq off from the Gulf coast.

steps.title: Karbala 5 and the Tanker War
steps.text: Iran's largest attempt on Basra, Karbala 5, broke into the outer defences around Fish Lake but stalled with enormous losses on both sides. In the Gulf, attacks on shipping drew in the superpowers: the US reflagged Kuwaiti tankers and escorted convoys, and an Iraqi missile struck the frigate USS Stark.

events.name: Operation Karbala 5
events.text: Iran gained ground east of Basra but could not take the city.

events.name: USS Stark incident
events.text: An Iraqi Exocet missile killed 37 US sailors, and Iraq called it a mistake.

steps.label: Mar to Aug 1988
steps.title: Iraq's final offensives and the ceasefire
steps.text: In March 1988 Iraqi aircraft gassed the Kurdish town of Halabja, killing thousands, during the Anfal campaign. From April Iraqi forces, led by the Republican Guard, retook Faw and drove Iran from its positions east of Basra and elsewhere, while US warships destroyed Iranian naval forces. On 18 July Iran accepted UN Resolution 598 and a ceasefire took effect on 20 August 1988.

events.name: Halabja chemical attack
events.text: Iraqi chemical bombs killed an estimated 3,000 to 5,000 Kurdish civilians.

events.name: Second Battle of al-Faw
events.text: Iraq recaptured the peninsula in about 36 hours.

events.name: UN Resolution 598 ceasefire
events.text: The ceasefire left the pre-war border in place.

name: Falklands War
summary: On 2 April 1982 Argentina's military government seized the British-ruled Falkland Islands, which it claims as the Malvinas, and South Georgia. Britain sent a naval task force 13,000 km south, retook South Georgia, landed at San Carlos and advanced across East Falkland until the Argentine garrison at Stanley surrendered on 14 June. About 650 Argentine and 255 British servicemen and three islanders died, and defeat hastened the fall of Argentina's junta.

steps.label: 2 to 3 Apr 1982
steps.title: Argentina takes the islands
steps.text: Argentine marines and special forces landed near Stanley in Operation Rosario and, after a short fight with the small Royal Marines garrison, Governor Rex Hunt surrendered. South Georgia was taken the next day. The UN Security Council demanded Argentine withdrawal, and Britain began assembling a task force.

events.name: Invasion of the Falklands
events.text: The garrison at Government House surrendered after a few hours.

events.name: Invasion of South Georgia
events.text: Royal Marines at Grytviken damaged a corvette before surrendering.

steps.label: Apr to mid May 1982
steps.title: The task force sails south
steps.text: Carriers and amphibious ships sailed from Portsmouth on 5 April and staged through Ascension Island while diplomacy failed. British forces retook South Georgia on 25 April. On 2 May the submarine HMS Conqueror sank the cruiser General Belgrano with 323 lives lost, after which the Argentine fleet stayed in port, and two days later an air-launched Exocet wrecked the destroyer HMS Sheffield.

events.name: Recapture of South Georgia
events.text: The Argentine garrison at Grytviken surrendered without a fight on land.

events.name: Sinking of the General Belgrano
events.text: The deadliest single loss of the war.

events.name: Sinking of HMS Sheffield
events.text: An Exocet missile set the destroyer ablaze, killing 20 crew.

steps.label: 21 May to 10 Jun 1982
steps.title: San Carlos and the advance
steps.text: 3 Commando Brigade under Brig. Julian Thompson landed at San Carlos Water on 21 May, and Argentine pilots sank several British ships in the anchorage in the following days. 2 Para won at Goose Green, then the commandos and paratroops marched across the north of East Falkland to the hills west of Stanley, while 5 Infantry Brigade moved by sea to Fitzroy, where air attacks hit the landing ships Sir Galahad and Sir Tristram.

events.name: San Carlos landings
events.text: About 4,000 troops got ashore, though air attacks sank HMS Ardent, Antelope and Coventry and the Atlantic Conveyor nearby.

events.name: Battle of Goose Green
events.text: 2 Para took the settlement and over 900 prisoners, its commander H. Jones being killed.

events.name: Bluff Cove air attacks
events.text: Bombs on two landing ships killed 48 British servicemen.

steps.label: 11 to 14 Jun 1982
steps.title: The fall of Stanley
steps.text: In night attacks British battalions took Mount Longdon, Two Sisters and Mount Harriet on 11 to 12 June, then Wireless Ridge and Mount Tumbledown on 13 to 14 June. With the high ground lost, Brig. Gen. Mario Menéndez surrendered the garrison of over 9,000 men to Maj. Gen. Jeremy Moore on 14 June. Galtieri was removed days later.

events.name: Battle of Mount Longdon
events.text: 3 Para took the mountain in the costliest British action of the war.

events.name: Battle of Mount Tumbledown
events.text: The Scots Guards cleared Argentine marines from the last key height.

events.name: Argentine surrender at Stanley
events.text: The surrender ended the fighting after 74 days.

name: Gulf War
summary: Iraq invaded and annexed Kuwait in August 1990 amid disputes over debt, oil prices and borders. A US-led coalition of 35 countries, authorised by the UN, built up forces in Saudi Arabia, waged a six-week air campaign from January 1991 and liberated Kuwait in a 100-hour ground offensive. Saddam Hussein stayed in power under sanctions, and the war set the pattern for later US involvement in the region.

steps.label: 2 Aug 1990
steps.title: Iraq invades Kuwait
steps.text: Republican Guard divisions crossed the border before dawn on 2 August and reached Kuwait City within hours, while helicopter-borne commandos attacked the Dasman Palace. The emir escaped to Saudi Arabia, the UN imposed sanctions, and Iraq declared Kuwait its nineteenth province.

events.name: Invasion of Kuwait
events.text: Kuwait's small army was overrun in less than two days.

events.name: Battle of the Dasman Palace
events.text: The emir's brother was killed defending the palace.

steps.label: Aug 1990 to Jan 1991
steps.title: Desert Shield
steps.text: Fearing a move on the Saudi oil fields, the US rushed troops to Saudi Arabia from 7 August, and a coalition of 35 countries eventually massed about 700,000 troops there. Iraq fortified Kuwait with minefields and trenches. UN Resolution 678 authorised force if Iraq had not left by 15 January 1991.

events.name: Operation Desert Shield
events.text: The first US units arrived in Dhahran within days of the invasion.

events.name: UN Resolution 678
events.text: The Security Council set a deadline of 15 January 1991.

steps.label: 17 Jan to 23 Feb 1991
steps.title: The air war
steps.text: Operation Desert Storm opened on 17 January with strikes on Baghdad, air defences and command centres, followed by weeks of bombing of Iraqi forces in Kuwait. Iraq fired Scud missiles at Israel and Saudi Arabia, set Kuwaiti oil wells alight and released oil into the Gulf. An Iraqi thrust into the Saudi town of Khafji was thrown back, while coalition armies shifted secretly west for an outflanking attack.

events.name: Air campaign begins
events.text: Cruise missiles and stealth aircraft struck Baghdad on the first night.

events.name: Battle of Khafji
events.text: Saudi, Qatari and US forces retook the town after two days.

events.name: Scud attacks on Israel
events.text: Israel did not retaliate, keeping Arab states in the coalition.

steps.label: 24 to 28 Feb 1991
steps.title: The 100-hour ground war
steps.text: US Marines and Arab forces breached the defences into Kuwait while the XVIII Airborne Corps swung deep into Iraq to the Euphrates and VII Corps hooked east to destroy Republican Guard divisions. Iraqi forces fled Kuwait City along the road north, where aircraft attacked their columns. Kuwait was liberated on 27 February and a ceasefire took effect the next day.

moves.label: XVIII Airborne Corps to the Euphrates

events.name: Battle of 73 Easting
events.text: US and British armour destroyed a Republican Guard division in a sandstorm.

events.name: Liberation of Kuwait City
events.text: Arab coalition forces entered the capital on 27 February.

events.name: Safwan ceasefire talks
events.text: Coalition and Iraqi generals agreed the terms of the ceasefire on 3 March.

steps.label: Mar to Apr 1991
steps.title: Uprisings and aftermath
steps.text: Shia rebels in the south and Kurds in the north rose against the government, but the Republican Guard crushed both uprisings within weeks, and over a million Kurds fled toward Turkey and Iran. The coalition set up a safe haven and later no-fly zones, while UN sanctions and weapons inspections continued through the 1990s.

events.name: 1991 uprisings
events.text: Rebels briefly held most southern cities and Kurdistan before being defeated.

events.name: Safe haven in northern Iraq
events.text: Coalition troops protected returning Kurdish refugees around Zakho.

name: Yugoslav Wars
summary: As Yugoslavia broke apart, a series of wars was fought between 1991 and 2001 over which peoples and lands would belong to which new states. Serbia under Slobodan Milosevic and Serb forces fought to keep Serb-inhabited areas in a common state, against Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia's government and later Kosovo Albanian rebels, with NATO intervening in Bosnia and Kosovo. The wars killed about 130,000 people, displaced millions and included the Srebrenica genocide, the worst atrocity in Europe since 1945.

sides.name: Serbia, the Yugoslav army and Serb forces
Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnian government and Kosovo Albanian forces

steps.label: Jun to Jul 1991
steps.title: Slovenia's Ten-Day War
steps.text: Slovenia and Croatia declared independence on 25 June 1991. When the Yugoslav People's Army (JNA) moved to seize Slovenia's border posts, Slovenian territorial defence forces blockaded and ambushed its columns. After ten days of fighting the European Community brokered the Brioni Agreement, and the JNA withdrew from Slovenia.

events.name: Ten-Day War
events.text: Slovenia secured its independence at a cost of a few dozen dead.

events.name: Brioni Agreement
events.text: A three-month moratorium led to the JNA's withdrawal from Slovenia.

steps.label: Aug 1991 to Jan 1992
steps.title: War in Croatia
steps.text: Croatian Serb rebels, backed by the JNA and Serbian volunteers, took about a third of Croatia, proclaiming the Republic of Serbian Krajina. The JNA destroyed and captured Vukovar after an 87-day siege and shelled Dubrovnik. A UN-brokered ceasefire in January 1992 froze the front lines under UN peacekeepers, and the European Community recognised Croatia and Slovenia.

events.name: Siege of Vukovar
events.text: The town fell on 18 November and about 200 prisoners were killed at Ovcara.

events.name: Siege of Dubrovnik
events.text: The old city was shelled but held, and the siege was lifted in 1992.

events.name: Sarajevo ceasefire
events.text: The Vance plan ceasefire took effect on 3 January 1992.

steps.label: Apr 1992 to 1994
steps.title: War in Bosnia
steps.text: Bosnia-Herzegovina declared independence after a referendum boycotted by most Serbs, and in April 1992 Bosnian Serb forces under Gen. Ratko Mladić, with JNA support, seized about 70 percent of the country, expelling and killing non-Serbs in the Drina valley and around Prijedor. Sarajevo was besieged and shelled for almost four years. In 1993 Bosnian Croat and government forces also fought each other until the US-brokered Washington Agreement of 1994.

fronts.label: Approximate front around government and Croat-held central Bosnia

moves.label: Bosnian Serb army in the east

events.name: Siege of Sarajevo
events.text: About 11,000 people were killed in the longest siege of a capital in modern history.

events.name: Prijedor camps
events.text: Bosniaks and Croats were held in camps such as Omarska, where many were killed.

events.name: Destruction of the Mostar bridge
events.text: Bosnian Croat shelling brought down the 16th-century Old Bridge during the Croat-Bosniak war.

steps.label: Jul to Aug 1995
steps.title: Srebrenica and Operation Storm
steps.text: In July 1995 Bosnian Serb forces overran the UN safe area of Srebrenica and killed about 8,000 Bosniak men and boys, a crime later judged genocide by international courts. In August the Croatian army under Gen. Ante Gotovina retook almost all of the Krajina in Operation Storm, and some 150,000 to 200,000 Serbs fled. Croatian and Bosnian forces then advanced in western Bosnia, together with the Bosnian 5th Corps breaking out of Bihać.

events.name: Srebrenica genocide
events.text: Some 8,000 Bosniak men and boys were killed after the enclave fell on 11 July.

events.name: Operation Storm
events.text: Croatia retook Knin and the Krajina in four days.

steps.label: Aug to Dec 1995
steps.title: NATO bombing and Dayton
steps.text: After a mortar attack on Sarajevo's Markale market, NATO bombed Bosnian Serb positions in Operation Deliberate Force, and Croatian and Bosnian offensives took more ground. A ceasefire followed in October, and talks at Dayton, Ohio produced an agreement signed in Paris in December. Bosnia remained one state of two entities, a Bosniak-Croat federation and the Republika Srpska, policed by a NATO-led force.

events.name: Operation Deliberate Force
events.text: Two weeks of air strikes hit Bosnian Serb artillery, ammunition and communications.

events.name: Dayton Agreement
events.text: The agreement ended the Bosnian War after about 100,000 deaths.

steps.label: 1998 to Jun 1999
steps.title: Kosovo
steps.text: Fighting between the Kosovo Liberation Army and Yugoslav and Serbian forces escalated in 1998. After the Racak killings and failed talks at Rambouillet, NATO began a 78-day air campaign against Yugoslavia on 24 March 1999, during which Serbian forces drove some 800,000 Kosovo Albanians into Albania and Macedonia. Milosevic accepted terms in June, Yugoslav forces withdrew, and a NATO-led force entered Kosovo under UN administration.

events.name: Racak massacre
events.text: The killing of 45 Albanian civilians in January 1999 hardened Western policy.

events.name: NATO bombing of Yugoslavia
events.text: Air strikes on military targets and infrastructure lasted from March to June.

events.name: Kumanovo Agreement
events.text: Yugoslav forces agreed to leave Kosovo.

steps.label: 2000 to 2001
steps.title: The last conflicts
steps.text: Milosevic was ousted after disputed elections in October 2000 and later handed to the Hague tribunal. Fighting flared in the Presevo valley of southern Serbia and in 2001 in Macedonia, where the ethnic Albanian National Liberation Army fought government forces until the Ohrid Agreement in August 2001 expanded Albanian minority rights, ending the Yugoslav Wars.

events.name: Overthrow of Milosevic
events.text: Mass protests in Belgrade forced Milosevic to concede defeat.

events.name: Ohrid Agreement
events.text: The deal ended the insurgency in Macedonia.

name: Rwandan Civil War and genocide
summary: The Rwandan Patriotic Front, formed mainly by Tutsi refugees in Uganda, invaded Rwanda in 1990 to fight the Hutu-led government of Juvenal Habyarimana. A peace deal in 1993 collapsed when Habyarimana's plane was shot down in April 1994, and extremists in the government, army and Interahamwe militia carried out a genocide that killed an estimated 500,000 to 800,000 people, mostly Tutsi. The RPF's victory in July ended the genocide, while some two million Hutu fled to Zaire, setting the stage for the Congo wars.

steps.label: Oct 1990
steps.title: The RPF invades
steps.text: On 1 October 1990 about 4,000 RPF fighters under Fred Rwigyema crossed from Uganda at Kagitumba. Rwigyema was killed on the second day, and Rwandan troops, backed by French, Belgian and Zairean forces, drove the rebels back. Paul Kagame returned from the US to take command and regrouped the RPF in the Virunga mountains.

events.name: RPF invasion
events.text: The first RPF offensive was defeated within weeks.

steps.label: 1991 to 1993
steps.title: Guerrilla war and the Arusha Accords
steps.text: The RPF fought a guerrilla war in the north, raiding Ruhengeri in January 1991, while Hutu extremist media and militias spread hatred of Tutsi. An RPF offensive in February 1993 pushed to within about 30 km of Kigali before a ceasefire. The Arusha Accords of August 1993 provided for power-sharing, and a UN force under Gen. Roméo Dallaire arrived to oversee it.

events.name: Ruhengeri raid
events.text: The RPF briefly took the town and freed prisoners from its jail.

events.name: Arusha Accords
events.text: The deal provided for a transitional government and a merged army.

steps.label: Apr to Jun 1994
steps.title: Genocide and the RPF offensive
steps.text: On 6 April 1994 President Habyarimana's plane was shot down over Kigali. Within hours the Presidential Guard, army units and Interahamwe militia began killing Tutsi and moderate Hutu across the country, organised under figures such as Col. Théoneste Bagosora, while the UN force was reduced. The RPF resumed its offensive, linking up with its battalion in Kigali and sweeping east and south.

events.name: President's plane shot down
events.text: The attack, whose perpetrators are still disputed, triggered the genocide.

events.name: Nyamata church massacre
events.text: Thousands who sheltered in the church were killed, one of many such massacres.

events.name: Siege of Kigali
events.text: The RPF fought for the capital from April to early July.

steps.label: Jul 1994
steps.title: RPF victory and exodus
steps.text: The RPF captured Kigali on 4 July and pushed west to Gisenyi, declaring the war over on 18 July. A French-led force set up a zone in the southwest under Operation Turquoise, and about two million Hutu, including many of those responsible for the genocide, fled into Zaire, where refugee camps around Goma became a base for further conflict.

events.name: Fall of Kigali
events.text: The capture of the capital effectively ended the genocide in RPF-held areas.

events.name: Operation Turquoise
events.text: French troops created a humanitarian zone in the southwest.

events.name: Exodus to Goma
events.text: Around a million refugees crossed into Goma within days, where cholera killed thousands.
